title: Born Again, A Language Odyssey
author: Andrew Ellison
summary: Language learning becomes truly miraculous not at first acquisition but in second-language and continued learning, where the already-conscious mind can witness its own transformation from incomprehension to understanding. The key to keeping our relationship with language vital and alive is repeatedly encountering the familiar in new linguistic contexts, forcing ourselves to be born again into language. When learners approach new languages through material already deeply known to them, their existing knowledge transcends weak language skills while new vocabulary becomes inferrable from context, creating explosive gains in both comprehension and linguistic fluency.
points: The miracle of language acquisition cannot be experienced in first-language learning, as consciousness emerges only after language takes root; it is uniquely accessible in second-language learning where reflection can accompany the learning process.

Learners make the fastest gains when attacking already-familiar material in a new language, as prior knowledge of content allows comprehension to transcend limited language skills and accelerates vocabulary acquisition through inferential context.

Keeping language healthy and vital requires deliberately encountering the familiar in new linguistic contexts through reading poetry, attending liturgies in different languages, and consuming familiar media in translation.
The routinization of language into mere transaction and habit can calcify one's relationship to speech unless actively renewed through conscious engagement and playful linguistic experimentation.
quotes: Unlike the miracle of physical birth, the wonder of language acquisition can be directly experienced, most drastically in second language acquisition, when the already-existing capacity for thought and reflection can be brought to bear by the learner upon the new learning.

Learning any language at all is a miraculous occurrence, a small thing that finds its best analogue in the event of the entire universe bursting into being ex nihilo. It is a leap that shouldn't be possible, understanding emerging where there had been only incomprehension before.

But reading a familiar story like 2001 in a foreign language in which I was still struggling seemed to produce gains that defied fundamental physical laws of energy conservation. My understanding of the already-familiar story transcended the limitations of my weak German.
When learning a new language, nothing can make you feel like you are making progress more rapidly than to attack something in a new language with which you are already familiar in your old one.

How are we to keep our love affair with language alive? Read poetry, especially the poetry of form and rhyme. Read English prose from the eighteenth century and earlier.” Archived from Classical Ed Review on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
